PSY300 MCQ — Instructor Dashboard

Anonymous response analytics. Data is read live from your Google Sheet via the Apps Script web app.

An app or the quiz opened once with ?rolle=underviser tags that browser as the instructor from then on (until it is opened with ?rolle=student). Those rows are excluded by default, so classroom demos and your own testing do not distort the student statistics.

Per-chapter mastery

Colour = the grade the proportion correct would give, using the grade boundaries in the Scores and grades tab (A 88, B 80, C 70, D 60, E 52 % by default) — so the scale is discrete and runs from the E–F boundary to the A boundary, and the letter is written in the cell. Change a boundary there and this map follows. Anything below the E boundary is F: the measured guessing floor is 36.4 % of the items in play, so a proportion down there says the material is not learnt, not how far below it is. Each cell also shows how many items in the chapter have been answered, and how many students are behind the number — 300 answers from four students is nothing like 300 answers from sixty. Hover a cell for the number of answers. Chapters with fewer than 20 students should be read with caution. Colour by switches both this map and the concept table between the grade scale and a percentage scale in fixed ten-point bands: under 50 %, then 50–60, 60–70, 70–80, 80–90 and 90–100. The bands are the way to read a colour off a round number, and to see the difference between two chapters that fall on either side of a boundary the grade scale does not draw. Everything under 50 % is one colour: that band already contains the measured guessing floor of 36.4 % — not 25 %, because one in four assumes all four options are live, and across the items with at least 10 answers an average of 3.06 of the 4 options are ever chosen; the floor is the mean of 1/m over the items, 36.4 % — not 1/3.06. Below the floor the proportion no longer says how much weaker a chapter is. Note the cost of fixed bands: the concepts currently span 42–80 %, so three of the six bands hold almost everything.

Item analysis

One row per item: how hard it turned out, whether the tag fits, how well it separates strong from weak students, and how the distractors were used. Mismatch = the Easy/Moderate/Hard tag likely needs updating (Easy ≥80%, Moderate 50–80%, Hard <50%). low D = discrimination below 0.2; the item barely separates. Click a header to sort; hover an ID to read the question.

IDChTag N% correct β SuggestedΔ repeatsD Distractor use Median s< 5 s Flags

Calibrate on first attempts. A student who practises the same item three times contributes three rows, and the second and third come after the explanation has been read — so the item looks easier than it is, and the rows are not independent. The default therefore counts each student once per item. Δ repeats is how many percentage points the item gains when repeats are included: a large positive value means the item is being learned rather than sampled. D = % correct among the top 27% of scorers minus the bottom 27%. Median s = median time from the question appearing to the first option being chosen, counted only while the tab was visible. < 5 s = share of answers given in under five seconds, a sign of guessing.

Errors & concepts

Chapters are a coarse unit — chapter 8 holds slope, R², residuals and moderation at once. Every item is therefore also tagged with the concepts it tests, and an item can carry several. The tagging is rule-based and readable in build_concept_tags.py, so a surprising row is worth checking against the items behind it before you rebuild a lecture around it.

% correct is pooled across every answer to every item carrying the concept, so a concept with few items rests on a narrow base — read the Items and Participants columns before acting. An item with three concepts counts in all three. Participants is the largest number of distinct anonymous codes seen on any single item in the concept: a lower bound on how many people the percentage rests on, since one person answering ten items must not count as ten. Answers given without a code are in the Answers column but not here.

«Trap» sorts by how far the most-chosen wrong option runs ahead of the correct one. A positive number means the distractor won: the class did not merely miss the item, it agreed on a specific wrong idea, which is the kind of error worth a slide.

Progress over time

One line per concept, pooled across the whole cohort — not one line per student. Each point is the proportion correct on the items carrying that concept, among all answers given in that week or at that attempt number. Points resting on fewer than 20 answers are left out, so a line with gaps means the cohort simply had not met those items yet. The chips below the plot give the number of answers and the number of students behind each line, and the vertical bar through each point is a 95 % interval computed with the student as the unit (a filled band when a single concept is isolated) — hover a point for its own numbers. This is the view that shows whether a concept actually improved after the lecture that covered it.

One line per anonymous code. Codes are never shown — students are numbered in the order they first appeared. Only attempts with at least 5 answers are plotted.

MCQ app use over the semester

The same figure as in the funding application: answers per week as bars against the left axis, active codes per week as a line against the right axis. The two measure different things, and the gap between them is the point. Answers say how much the app was used; active codes say by how many. When the bars grow faster than the line, the same students are practising more — it is not that more students have joined.

Rasch model: progress with student and item held fixed

The raw proportion correct over the semester is misleading, because both who answers and which items they meet change from week to week. This tab fits an explanatory Rasch model — a logistic mixed model with one term per student and one per item as random effects, and semester week as a fixed effect: logit P(correct) = μ + θstudent − βitem + γ·week. The time term γ is therefore the progress that remains once the composition of both students and items is held constant. Fitting takes a few seconds; press the button.

Item difficulty

β on the logit scale, with the cohort's average student as the reference. A high value means the item is hard after accounting for who happened to answer it — which is not the same as a low raw proportion correct. The ten hardest and the ten easiest with at least ten answers.

Items that do not fit the model

The Rasch model assumes every item discriminates equally; it never checks. Infit and outfit are mean squared standardised residuals, expected 1. Above 1.3 means more noise than the model allows — guessing, an ambiguous stem, or an item measuring something else. Below 0.7 means too predictable: the item repeats what its neighbours already measure. Infit is information-weighted and is the one to read first; outfit is driven by single surprises. Read MNSQ together with t: with a large n, a harmless 1.05 can still give t = 3. The statistics are in-sample — θ and β are fitted on the same answers the residuals are computed from, roughly one parameter per seven observations — so both sit below 1 on this bank (mean infit 0.89). Compare items with each other; the 0.7–1.3 convention is borrowed from marginal estimates and does not transfer directly.

When and how the app is used

Weekday, time of day, and how often the same item is answered again. The attempt distribution is the basis for the first-attempt rule used everywhere else in this dashboard: by the third attempt the cohort gets 84 % right, so counting every answer measures practice rather than difficulty.

Simulation use (anonymous)

One session = one opening of an app. Time counts only while the tab is visible, capped at 30 s between heartbeats, so a forgotten tab does not inflate the numbers. No codes, names or IP addresses are involved. Sessions with no close signal (browser killed) appear as unfinished and are counted with 0 s.
